PlayCanvas is an open-source game engine built on WebGL2 and WebGPU. Use it to create interactive 3D apps, games and visualizations that run in any browser on any device.
Unreal is a bloated way to develop WebGPU projects for the web. PlayCanvas is a sensible solution if your target is web.
I think Playcanvas would do well to focus on the basics, like being able to export/import variables in the standard js way, being able to develop offline, using your own source control.

If you really get into the nitty gritty of PC it becomes quickly apparent there's some very strange design choices and priorities. You can produce some great stuff but there are many dev-exp headaches.
ES6 Modules and NPM support is actively being worked on and should be ready by end of year - Typescript support will follow after that (from ex-PlayCanvas employee).
Venge.io is probably one of the most impressive games I've played in the browser, and was built using PlayCanvas.
Every time I've taken a look at this engine it has always felt very limited. And with a $15/month subscription just to be able to create private projects I just can't justify it personally.
It is a very nice engine, specially for those focused on Web only as target.

We looked at this as an engine for a project. At the time we decided not to go with it since all your code needs to live on their server and there's no easy local dev environment... too risky a proposition (what if they go out of business tomorrow?) and too limiting for the cost they were asking.
I'd love to be able to use their scene editor offline, uploading assets is a deal breaker.
I recommend checking out the newly released playcanvas-sync tools which let you map your PlayCanvas project's assets to your local machine's file system.
An example of what could be done with it: venge.io - A competitive FPS shooter made in Playcanvas.
THREE.js is very low-level framework, while PlayCanvas additionally to low-level engine access has game framework, which will allow you to create game logic and scripting in much better way.
I analyzed their JS math library (2013) and was pleasantly surprised (optimized, lean object design). Love what PlayCanvas is doing. They seem committed to the community and their people.
It's an open source javascript game engine that is kinda like halfway between something like three.js and e.g. Unity—pretty lightweight, but still comes with a nice scene editor etc.
